findings: Chapter 12 of the 3rd edition, Designing and Deploying Command Line Programs, is new in this edition and teaches how to run Python programs outside the code editor: the vocabulary of program, script, command, shell script, application, app and web app; the terminal, with the cd, pwd, dir and ls commands, running programs and opening files by name; the PATH environment variable, how Windows, macOS and Linux search it, how to add a Scripts folder to it, and the which and where commands; virtual environments made with python -m venv .venv, activated, deactivated and kept away from the system Python; pip run as python -m pip to install, list, upgrade, pin and uninstall packages from PyPI, and the automateboringstuff3 package; the built-in values __file__, sys.executable, sys.version, sys.version_info, os.name and sys.platform and the ModuleNotFoundError check; text-based program design - short command names, command line arguments in sys.argv with argparse left to its documentation, clipboard input and output with pyperclip, colourful text with Bext, clearing the terminal with os.system, sound with playsound3 and verbose and quiet modes; the Snowstorm animation; PyMsgBox's alert, confirm, prompt and password; deployment with a batch file on Windows, a .command file on macOS and a shell script with a .desktop entry on Ubuntu; the ccwd and Clipboard Recorder programs; PyInstaller's --onefile build; and it closes with a summary, 6 practice questions and one practice program.

The chapter's command line examples reproduce under Python 3.14.6: a script run as python3 yourScript.py hello world received ['yourScript.py', 'hello', 'world'] and with the two words in quotation marks ['yourScript.py', 'hello world']; __file__ was an absolute path even when the script was started by a relative name, which is what the chapter prints and what Python 3.9 made the rule; os.name was 'posix' and sys.platform 'linux'; list(sys.version_info) gave [3, 14, 6, 'final', 0], where the chapter's own printed list, [3, 13, 1 'final', 0], lacks the comma after the 1, a typing slip and not a different value.

python -m venv .venv under Python 3.14.6 made a .venv folder with bin/activate, a pyvenv.cfg holding include-system-site-packages = false, and, new since Python 3.13, a .gitignore; python -m pip list in the fresh environment listed pip 26.1.2 alone, whereas the chapter's listing shows pip 23.0 and setuptools 65.5.0, which is what a Python before 3.12 installed, since Python 3.12 venv no longer pre-installs setuptools (gh-95299); inside the environment sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix was True and outside it False, the test the venv documentation gives for detecting an environment.

The chapter's Ubuntu deployment was executed: a shell script launcher named yourScript, starting with #!/usr/bin/env bash and sourcing ~/Scripts/.venv/bin/activate, was made executable with chmod u+x (its mode became -rwxr--r--), found by shutil.which in a folder on PATH and run by name, and the script ran inside the virtual environment; but the chapter's macOS and Linux launchers run python3 ~/Scripts/yourScript.py with nothing after it, so yourScript spam eggs reached the script with sys.argv holding only its own path, and adding '$@' to that line forwarded spam and eggs, which the Windows batch file does with %*. The online chapter also prints two options with an en dash in place of a hyphen: read ... -n1 –s in its launchers, which bash rejected with read: `–s': not a valid identifier and exit status 1, and python –m venv and python –m pip in its prose, which Python 3.14.6 took as a file name and refused (can't open file).

The chapter's ccwd.py and cliprec.py were run unchanged in subprocesses with a stand-in pyperclip module, because this machine has no clipboard and the real pyperclip 1.11.0 raised PyperclipException (could not find a copy/paste mechanism): ccwd copied ~/Scripts, and ccwd .. copied ~, while the shell that started it still printed ~/Scripts for pwd, which is the chapter's point that os.chdir() changes only the program's own working directory; cliprec printed each new clipboard text once, skipped repeats and ended quietly when KeyboardInterrupt was raised inside its try block; KeyboardInterrupt is not a subclass of Exception, so an except Exception clause would not have caught CTRL-C.

The chapter's third-party packages were installed from PyPI and inspected, not run against a display or speaker: Bext 0.1.1 offers fg, bg, clear, width, height, title, goto and get_key as printed, but its cursor functions are hide_cursor and show_cursor rather than the hide and show the chapter lists; PyMsgBox 2.0.1 offers alert, confirm, prompt and password; playsound3 3.3.2 offers playsound, as the chapter's prose says, but the automateboringstuff3 2024.10.1 package, which the chapter recommends for the book's exact versions, requires playsound==1.3.0, the older package with a different name.

PyInstaller 6.22.3, installed into a virtual environment under Python 3.14.6, built python -m PyInstaller --onefile hello.py for a one-line, 23-byte Hello, world program in about 15 seconds, left a build folder, a dist folder and a hello.spec file, and the one executable in dist was 12,950,120 bytes and printed Hello, world!, larger than the chapter's close to 8MB, which describes Windows; python -m pyinstaller in lower case failed with No module named pyinstaller, as the chapter warns, and the PyInstaller manual states that its output is specific to the operating system and the Python version it runs under.

For an advanced course, chapter 12 is best taught as the path a typed command takes to a running program: the terminal searches PATH, a launcher script activates a virtual environment and starts the interpreter, the interpreter hands the words to sys.argv, and the program reports back through its output and its exit code; the chapter's outputs hold under 3.14.6 except the setuptools line of its pip list, its macOS and Linux launchers need '$@' to forward arguments, its en-dash options must be typed as hyphens, and Bext's cursor functions and the playsound pin differ from its text, while argparse, PEP 668, the sys.prefix test for an environment and the measured size of a PyInstaller build are what the course adds.

Current Python and current systems add to the chapter: PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its system Python as externally managed, and on this Ubuntu 24.04 machine python3.12 -m pip install pyperclip stopped with error: externally-managed-environment, so the chapter's advice to keep packages out of the system Python is now enforced; the pip user guide recommends python -m pip for the same reason the chapter gives; argparse, which the chapter leaves to its documentation, declares arguments, converts types and writes usage errors, and in Python 3.14 colours its help text and can suggest a mistyped choice; shlex.split() splits a command line the way a POSIX shell does, and shutil.which() answers the question the which and where commands answer.
title: Command line programs for an advanced course: chapter 12 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Terminal
nodes.body: Chapter 12 starts where every earlier chapter stopped, at the point where a program has to run without the code editor that wrote it, and it starts with the terminal, the text window in which a program is started by typing its name (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter calls deployment the process of making software usable outside the editor, and the terminal is the first place that happens.

paras.text: Chapter 12 starts where every earlier chapter stopped, at the point where a program has to run without the code editor that wrote it, and it starts with the terminal, the text window in which a program is started by typing its name (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter calls deployment the process of making software usable outside the editor, and the terminal is the first place that happens.

Three ideas carry this subject. Program vocabulary separates the many words that all mean some kind of program, from a script to a web app. Navigating folders covers the commands that move the terminal around the file system and run what is there. The PATH variable covers how the terminal finds a program by its bare name, which is what later lets a deployed launcher run from any folder at all.

nodes.label: Program vocabulary
nodes.body: The chapter lists seven words that can all fairly be called a program, and the differences between them are about how the program is run rather than what it does: a program, a script, a command, a shell script, an application, an app and a web app (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The chapter lists seven words that can all fairly be called a program, and the differences between them are about how the program is run rather than what it does: a program, a script, a command, a shell script, an application, an app and a web app (Sweigart, 2025).

Interpreted script is the word for what this course writes: Python source run by the interpreter. Terminal command is the word for a program run by name from a terminal with its options given up front. Shell script is the word for a file of terminal commands, the form every launcher later in the chapter takes, whether it is a batch file on Windows or a shell script launcher on Ubuntu.

nodes.label: Interpreted script
nodes.body: A script is a program that an interpreter runs from its source code rather than from a compiled, machine-code form, a loose term that the chapter applies to Python programs although Python code can be bundled into an executable as well (Sweigart, 2025). Under Python 3.14.6, compile() turned the one-line source print(42), named yourScript.py, into a code object, which is the form the interpreter actually runs, so even an interpreted script is translated before it runs, only not into machine code (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A script is a program that an interpreter runs from its source code rather than from a compiled, machine-code form, a loose term that the chapter applies to Python programs although Python code can be bundled into an executable as well (Sweigart, 2025). Under Python 3.14.6, compile() turned the one-line source print(42), named yourScript.py, into a code object, which is the form the interpreter actually runs, so even an interpreted script is translated before it runs, only not into machine code (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

That distinction returns at the end of the chapter: the one file build of PyInstaller does not change what a script is, it ships the bundled interpreter together with the script. Running a script still needs that interpreter, which is why every launcher of the chapter starts by naming python or python3 and why the system interpreter, the one an operating system ships, matters to anyone who installs packages.

nodes.definition: A script is a program that an interpreter runs from its source code rather than from compiled machine code; Python programs are usually called scripts, although PyInstaller can bundle one into an executable file.

nodes.label: Terminal command
nodes.body: A command is a program that is often run from a text-based terminal and has no graphical user interface; everything it needs is given up front as command line arguments, although an interactive command may stop to ask a question such as Are you sure? Y/N (Sweigart, 2025). dir and ls, which list a folder, are the chapter's own examples, and cd and cp are others.

Y/N (Sweigart, 2025). dir and ls, which list a folder, are the chapter's own examples, and cd and cp are others.

A Python program becomes a command when a user can type its name in a terminal and give it arguments, which is exactly what the argv list delivers to the program and what the short command names advice is about. The chapter's ccwd script is such a command: four lines of Python behind a name of four letters, reached through a launcher in a folder on PATH.

nodes.definition: A command is a program run from a text-based terminal without a graphical user interface and configured up front by command line arguments, such as dir, ls, cd or cp.

nodes.label: Shell script
nodes.body: A shell script is a single text file that runs several terminal commands in one batch, so that a user runs one file instead of typing each command; on macOS and Linux it has a .sh extension or none, and Windows calls it a batch file, with the .bat extension (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A shell script is a single text file that runs several terminal commands in one batch, so that a user runs one file instead of typing each command; on macOS and Linux it has a .sh extension or none, and Windows calls it a batch file, with the .bat extension (Sweigart, 2025).

Every deployment in the chapter is a shell script. The batch file on Windows, the command file on macOS and the shell script launcher on Ubuntu each hold the same three steps - activate the virtual environment, run the script, deactivate - and on macOS and Linux the file must also carry the execute permission before the system will run it. On Linux its first line is a shebang line, which names the program that reads the rest.

nodes.definition: A shell script is one text file that runs several terminal commands in one batch; macOS and Linux use a .sh extension or none, and Windows calls it a batch file with the .bat extension.

nodes.label: Navigating folders
nodes.body: A terminal, like a running program, has a current working directory, and moving it, listing it and running what is in it are the three everyday jobs of the command line (Sweigart, 2025). The prompt itself shows the folder on Windows, macOS and Ubuntu, each in its own format.

paras.text: A terminal, like a running program, has a current working directory, and moving it, listing it and running what is in it are the three everyday jobs of the command line (Sweigart, 2025). The prompt itself shows the folder on Windows, macOS and Ubuntu, each in its own format.

Change directory covers cd and pwd and their Python twins, os.chdir() and os.getcwd(). List directory covers dir and ls and their Python twin, os.listdir(). Run from terminal covers starting a program, a script or an ordinary file by name or by path, the step that the PATH variable later makes possible from any folder.

nodes.label: Change directory
nodes.body: The terminal has a current working directory that relative paths are attached to; pwd on macOS and Linux, or cd with no argument on Windows, shows it, and cd followed by a relative or absolute path changes it, with cd .. moving up one folder and a drive letter followed by a colon switching drives on Windows (Sweigart, 2025). A Python program does the same with os.chdir() and os.getcwd() (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The terminal has a current working directory that relative paths are attached to; pwd on macOS and Linux, or cd with no argument on Windows, shows it, and cd followed by a relative or absolute path changes it, with cd .. moving up one folder and a drive letter followed by a colon switching drives on Windows (Sweigart, 2025). A Python program does the same with os.chdir() and os.getcwd() (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Run under Python 3.14.6, a program that changed into a new folder, made Desktop, changed into it and then into .. found itself in Desktop and then back where it started, exactly the walk the chapter types at the Windows prompt. What this concept does not change is the folder of the terminal that started the program: the program working directory concept and the ccwd script both turn on that point.

nodes.definition: cd changes the terminal's current working directory to a relative or absolute path, and pwd on macOS and Linux, or cd alone on Windows, shows it; a Python program does the same with os.chdir() and os.getcwd().

nodes.label: List directory
nodes.body: dir on Windows and ls on macOS and Linux list the files and subfolders of the current working directory, dir *.exe lists only the programs on Windows and file * | grep executable does the same on macOS and Linux (Sweigart, 2025). Inside Python, os.listdir() returns the same names as a list of strings, in no promised order (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: dir on Windows and ls on macOS and Linux list the files and subfolders of the current working directory, dir *.exe lists only the programs on Windows and file * | grep executable does the same on macOS and Linux (Sweigart, 2025). Run under Python 3.14.6 against a folder holding spam.exe, eggs.exe, notes.txt and a Scripts folder, the sorted listing named all four and a test on the .exe ending kept the two programs, the Python form of dir *.exe. Listing is how a user checks what is in a folder before running it from the terminal, and it is the first thing to try when a terminal command reports that a file is not there.

nodes.label: Run from terminal
nodes.body: A .py file runs by naming it after python on Windows or python3 on macOS and Linux, either by its absolute path or by a relative one from its own folder; a program in the current folder runs as example.exe on Windows but must be typed as ./example on macOS and Linux; and a file that is not a program, such as example.txt, opens in its associated application when its name is entered on Windows or after open on macOS (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A .py file runs by naming it after python on Windows or python3 on macOS and Linux, either by its absolute path or by a relative one from its own folder; a program in the current folder runs as example.exe on Windows but must be typed as ./example on macOS and Linux; and a file that is not a program, such as example.txt, opens in its associated application when its name is entered on Windows or after open on macOS (Sweigart, 2025).

Typing a full path every time is what the rest of the chapter removes. The PATH search order lets a bare name work from any folder, a shell script turns a long python3 command into one word, and the execute permission is what allows ./example, or a launcher found on PATH, to run at all on macOS and Linux.

nodes.definition: A .py file runs by naming it after python or python3 with an absolute or a relative path, a program in the current folder runs as example.exe on Windows but as ./example on macOS and Linux, and a file that is not a program opens in its associated application.

nodes.label: Path variable
nodes.body: Every running program has environment variables, and PATH, a list of folders, is the one the terminal reads to find a program from its bare name (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter's Ubuntu example lists eleven folders, from /home/al/.local/bin to /snap/bin, separated by colons.

paras.text: Every running program has environment variables, and PATH, a list of folders, is the one the terminal reads to find a program from its bare name (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter's Ubuntu example lists eleven folders, from /home/al/.local/bin to /snap/bin, separated by colons.

Path search order covers how the folders are searched and what is not searched. Path editing covers adding a Scripts folder so that a launcher kept there runs from anywhere. Which and where covers asking the terminal where a name will be found, the check the chapter uses both to debug PATH and to choose a free name for a new command.

nodes.label: Path search order
nodes.body: When a program name is typed, the terminal looks for it in the folders listed in PATH, one after another, and runs the first match; Windows first checks the current working directory and then PATH, whereas macOS and Linux check only PATH, which is why a program in the current folder must be typed as ./example there; and folders below a PATH folder are not searched (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: When a program name is typed, the terminal looks for it in the folders listed in PATH, one after another, and runs the first match; Windows first checks the current working directory and then PATH, whereas macOS and Linux check only PATH, which is why a program in the current folder must be typed as ./example there; and folders below a PATH folder are not searched (Sweigart, 2025).

A run under Python 3.14.6 modelled that rule with three PATH folders, a, b and c, where a held spam only in its subfolder sub: the search stopped at b, the first folder that itself held spam, and never looked into a/sub. Activating a venv works by exactly this rule, putting the environment's own folder first so that its python is the first match, and which and where report the match the rule would find.

nodes.definition: PATH is an environment variable holding a list of folders that the terminal searches in order for a typed program name; the first folder holding the name wins, subfolders are never searched, and Windows looks in the current folder first while macOS and Linux do not.

nodes.label: Path editing
nodes.body: To add a folder to PATH on Windows, the user variable Path is edited in the Environment Variables window, with a semicolon before the new folder; on macOS and Linux a line export PATH=/home/al/Scripts:$PATH is added to the bottom of .zshrc or .bashrc, the startup script every new terminal runs, so the change reaches only terminal windows opened afterwards (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: To add a folder to PATH on Windows, the user variable Path is edited in the Environment Variables window, with a semicolon before the new folder; on macOS and Linux a line export PATH=/home/al/Scripts:$PATH is added to the bottom of .zshrc or .bashrc, the startup script every new terminal runs, so the change reaches only terminal windows opened afterwards (Sweigart, 2025).

Run under Python 3.14.6, joining /home/al/Scripts in front of the existing folders with a colon gave the string the export line builds, the new folder first. A Scripts folder on PATH is what every launcher of the chapter relies on: the batch file, the command file and the shell script launcher are all kept there so that one short name starts them from any folder.

nodes.definition: A folder is added to PATH through the user variable Path in the Windows Environment Variables window, or with an export line at the bottom of .zshrc on macOS or .bashrc on Linux, which affects only terminal windows opened afterwards; folders are separated by a semicolon on Windows and a colon on macOS and Linux.

nodes.label: Which and where
nodes.body: which on macOS and Linux and where on Windows report the folder on PATH that holds a given program; where lists every match, and the topmost one is the program that runs when the name is typed (Sweigart, 2025). Inside Python, shutil.which() returns the path of the program that would run for a name, checking that it exists and is executable, or None (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: which on macOS and Linux and where on Windows report the folder on PATH that holds a given program; where lists every match, and the topmost one is the program that runs when the name is typed (Sweigart, 2025). Inside Python, shutil.which() returns the path of the program that would run for a name, checking that it exists and is executable, or None (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The chapter uses these commands for two jobs: finding which python a terminal will start, before and after activating a venv, and checking that a new command name is still free, the step that comes before choosing short command names such as ccwd. The deployment program of this course calls shutil.which() to confirm that its own launcher was found in the Scripts folder after that folder was put on PATH.

nodes.definition: which on macOS and Linux and where on Windows report the folder on PATH from which a program name would run; where lists every match, the topmost one is the one that runs, and shutil.which() answers the same question inside Python.

nodes.label: Environments
nodes.body: Two programs that need different versions of one package cannot share one Python installation, and the chapter's answer is the virtual environment, with pip as the tool that fills it from PyPI (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Two programs that need different versions of one package cannot share one Python installation, and the chapter's answer is the virtual environment, with pip as the tool that fills it from PyPI (Sweigart, 2025).

Virtual environments covers creating, activating and recognising an environment, and why packages stay out of the system Python. The pip installer covers what a package is, why pip is run through the interpreter, and the install, upgrade, pin, list and uninstall commands. Every launcher of the deployment subject activates the environment built here before it runs its script.

nodes.label: Virtual environments
nodes.body: A virtual environment is a separate installation of Python with its own set of installed third-party packages, made by the built-in venv module; the chapter advises one environment per application but allows one shared environment for small scripts while learning (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A virtual environment is a separate installation of Python with its own set of installed third-party packages, made by the built-in venv module; the chapter advises one environment per application but allows one shared environment for small scripts while learning (Sweigart, 2025).

Creating a venv covers the command and the folder it makes. Activating a venv covers what activation changes and how it is undone. Venv detection covers how a running program can tell that it is inside one. System interpreter covers the Python that ships with macOS and Linux and why packages should not be installed into it, a piece of advice that current systems now enforce.

nodes.label: Creating a venv
nodes.body: python -m venv .venv, typed in the Scripts folder, creates a virtual environment in a new folder named .venv, a conventional name whose leading period hides it; the environment starts with only the default packages and none of those installed in the original Python (Sweigart, 2025). PEP 405 made this part of Python 3.3, crediting Ian Bicking's virtualenv as the tool that proved the idea (Meyer, 2011).

PEP 405 made this part of Python 3.3, crediting Ian Bicking's virtualenv as the tool that proved the idea (Meyer, 2011).

Run under Python 3.14.6, the command made a .venv folder holding bin/activate, a pyvenv.cfg file with include-system-site-packages = false and, new since Python 3.13, a .gitignore, and python -m pip list inside it listed pip alone. The chapter's own listing shows pip 23.0 and setuptools 65.5.0, which is what a Python before 3.12 installed; since 3.12 venv no longer pre-installs setuptools (Python Software Foundation, 2026). nodes.definition: python -m venv .venv creates a virtual environment, a separate Python installation with its own set of installed packages, in a hidden folder named .venv by convention, so that two programs can depend on different versions of one package.

nodes.label: Activating a venv
nodes.body: Activation runs activate.bat in .venv\Scripts on Windows or source activate in .venv/bin on macOS and Linux; it changes PATH so that python or python3 runs the environment's interpreter and adds (.venv) to the prompt, in the current terminal window only, and deactivate, closing the window, or deleting the .venv folder ends it (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Activation runs activate.bat in .venv\Scripts on Windows or source activate in .venv/bin on macOS and Linux; it changes PATH so that python or python3 runs the environment's interpreter and adds (.venv) to the prompt, in the current terminal window only, and deactivate, closing the window, or deleting the .venv folder ends it (Sweigart, 2025).

Activation is path editing done for one window: the environment's own folder is put first, so the path search order finds its python before any other, which the chapter shows with where python.exe and which python3. The venv documentation adds that activation is a convenience, since running the environment's own python by its path works without it (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and every launcher of the deployment branch activates first and deactivates last.

nodes.definition: Activating an environment, with activate.bat on Windows or source activate on macOS and Linux, puts its folder first on PATH and adds (.venv) to the prompt in that one terminal window; deactivate undoes it, and deleting the .venv folder removes the environment with its packages.

nodes.label: Venv detection
nodes.body: A program can tell whether it runs inside a virtual environment, because there sys.prefix names the environment's folder while sys.base_prefix names the Python that created it; the venv documentation says that checking sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is sufficient (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and PEP 405 defines the rule through the pyvenv.cfg file (Meyer, 2011).

paras.text: A program can tell whether it runs inside a virtual environment, because there sys.prefix names the environment's folder while sys.base_prefix names the Python that created it; the venv documentation says that checking sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is sufficient (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and PEP 405 defines the rule through the pyvenv.cfg file (Meyer, 2011).

The chapter itself checks the environment from outside, with where and which; this test is the inside view a course adds. Under Python 3.14.6 it was False in the interpreter that builds this course and True in a fresh .venv, and the deployment program of this course prints it to prove that a shell script launcher really started the environment's python and not the system interpreter.

nodes.definition: Inside a virtual environment sys.prefix names the environment and sys.base_prefix the Python that created it, so a program can tell that it runs in one when the two differ; outside an environment they are equal.

nodes.label: System interpreter
nodes.body: macOS and Linux ship their own Python, called the system Python, for programs of the operating system; running scripts with it is fine, but installing or updating packages in it can introduce incompatibilities that break those programs, so a virtual environment in the Scripts folder is the chapter's precaution (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: macOS and Linux ship their own Python, called the system Python, for programs of the operating system; running scripts with it is fine, but installing or updating packages in it can introduce incompatibilities that break those programs, so a virtual environment in the Scripts folder is the chapter's precaution (Sweigart, 2025).

Current systems enforce that advice. PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its Python as externally managed (Thomas et al., 2021), and on the Ubuntu 24.04 machine that built this course, python3.12 -m pip install pyperclip stopped with error: externally-managed-environment, pointing to apt or a virtual environment instead. Creating a venv is therefore no longer only good practice on such a system but the way pip install works at all, and the chapter adds that the Mu editor keeps an environment of its own.

nodes.definition: The system Python is the installation that macOS and Linux ship for their own programs; running scripts with it is fine, installing packages into it can break those programs, and since PEP 668 distributions such as Ubuntu 24.04 refuse pip install there with error: externally-managed-environment.

nodes.label: Pip installer
nodes.body: pip, a recursive acronym for pip installs packages, is the command line package manager that comes with Python and downloads third-party packages from PyPI, the Python Package Index at pypi.org (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: pip, a recursive acronym for pip installs packages, is the command line package manager that comes with Python and downloads third-party packages from PyPI, the Python Package Index at pypi.org (Sweigart, 2025).

Packages and modules covers the two words the chapter separates. Running pip as a module covers why python -m pip is preferred to the pip program. Install and uninstall covers the five pip commands the chapter uses and the automateboringstuff3 package that pins the book's versions.

nodes.label: Packages and modules
nodes.body: In Python, a package is a collection of Python code made available on PyPI and a module is an individual .py file of Python code; packages are installed from PyPI, they contain modules, and an import statement imports a module (Sweigart, 2025). The standard library's modules, such as sys, random and os, need no installing.

paras.text: In Python, a package is a collection of Python code made available on PyPI and a module is an individual .py file of Python code; packages are installed from PyPI, they contain modules, and an import statement imports a module (Sweigart, 2025). The standard library's modules, such as sys, random and os, need no installing.

Under Python 3.14.6, the value an import produced, json in the example, was an object of type module. Install and uninstall covers how a package gets onto a computer, and the missing module check covers what a program can do when one has not been installed yet, catching ModuleNotFoundError instead of failing with a traceback.

nodes.example: python -m pip install pyperclip, then import pyperclip
nodes.definition: A package is a collection of Python code published on PyPI, the Python Package Index, and a module is one .py file of Python code; pip installs packages, which contain modules, and an import statement imports a module.

nodes.label: Running pip as a module
nodes.body: pip is a program of its own, but the chapter runs it through the interpreter, as python -m pip on Windows or python3 -m pip on macOS and Linux, because that installs into the very Python that python or python3 starts, avoiding the case where several installations exist, PATH is misconfigured and the pip program on PATH belongs to another one (Sweigart, 2025). The pip user guide recommends the same form (Python Packaging Authority, 2026).

paras.text: pip is a program of its own, but the chapter runs it through the interpreter, as python -m pip on Windows or python3 -m pip on macOS and Linux, because that installs into the very Python that python or python3 starts, avoiding the case where several installations exist, PATH is misconfigured and the pip program on PATH belongs to another one (Sweigart, 2025). The pip user guide recommends the same form (Python Packaging Authority, 2026).

The same reasoning explains why the chapter runs PyInstaller as python -m PyInstaller. The online chapter prints python -m in several prose passages with an en dash instead of a hyphen; Python 3.14.6 read that dash as a file name and refused with can't open file, so the option must be typed as a plain hyphen. Inside an activated venv, python -m pip installs into that environment only.

nodes.definition: Running pip through the interpreter, as python -m pip on Windows or python3 -m pip on macOS and Linux, installs into exactly the Python that python or python3 starts, which avoids a pip program on PATH that belongs to another installation.

nodes.label: Install and uninstall
nodes.body: python -m pip install package_name installs a package from PyPI, install -U upgrades it to the latest version, package_name==1.17.4 installs one exact version, uninstall removes it and list shows every installed package with its version; the chapter adds that Anaconda users should use conda instead, and that the automateboringstuff3 package installs the versions the book was written with (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: python -m pip install package_name installs a package from PyPI, install -U upgrades it to the latest version, package_name==1.17.4 installs one exact version, uninstall removes it and list shows every installed package with its version; the chapter adds that Anaconda users should use conda instead, and that the automateboringstuff3 package installs the versions the book was written with (Sweigart, 2025).

Run under Python 3.14.6, partitioning 'package_name==1.17.4' at == gave the name and the version a pin names. The automateboringstuff3 2024.10.1 package, read for this course, requires bext, pymsgbox, pyperclip and pyperclipimg without a version and playsound at exactly 1.3.0, which is the older package rather than the playsound3 the chapter's sound and text notification passage teaches. Installing into a venv keeps such pins away from the system interpreter.

nodes.definition: pip install adds a package from PyPI, install -U upgrades it, package_name==1.17.4 installs one exact version, uninstall removes it and list shows every installed package with its version; the automateboringstuff3 package installs the versions the book was written with.

nodes.label: Self aware
nodes.body: Several built-in values tell a running program about itself, the interpreter running it and the operating system, and the interpreter sets them automatically; the chapter calls such programs self-aware (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Several built-in values tell a running program about itself, the interpreter running it and the operating system, and the interpreter sets them automatically; the chapter calls such programs self-aware (Sweigart, 2025).

Script location covers __file__, sys.executable and sys.version. Platform checks covers sys.version_info, os.name and sys.platform, which let one program behave correctly on Windows, macOS and Linux. Module checks covers the ModuleNotFoundError test and sys.exit(), with which a program reports a missing package and stops with a clear message.

nodes.label: Script location
nodes.body: A program can ask where it is and what runs it: __file__ gives the path of its own .py file, and sys.executable and sys.version describe the interpreter (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A program can ask where it is and what runs it: __file__ gives the path of its own .py file, and sys.executable and sys.version describe the interpreter (Sweigart, 2025).

File variable covers __file__ and the Path(__file__) idiom for finding files kept beside a program. Interpreter location covers sys.executable and sys.version, the values that tell which installation, a venv's or the system interpreter, is running the program.

nodes.label: File variable
nodes.body: __file__ contains the running .py file's path as a string, Path(__file__) turns it into a Path object useful for finding files in the program's own folder, and the variable does not exist in the interactive shell (Sweigart, 2025). Since Python 3.9 it is an absolute path even when the script was started by a relative name, so it stays valid after os.chdir() (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: __file__ contains the running .py file's path as a string, Path(__file__) turns it into a Path object useful for finding files in the program's own folder, and the variable does not exist in the interactive shell (Sweigart, 2025). Since Python 3.9 it is an absolute path even when the script was started by a relative name, so it stays valid after os.chdir() (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Run under Python 3.14.6, a script started as python3 yourScript.py from its own folder printed an absolute path ending in yourScript.py, and code executed from a string had no __file__ at all, which is why the corpus programs of this course, which run from a string, write their scripts to files before they ask for it. A launcher that starts a script from another folder makes this matter: change directory has moved, the file has not.

nodes.definition: __file__ holds the running .py file's path as a string, an absolute path since Python 3.9, so Path(__file__).parent finds files kept beside the program; code that does not come from a file, such as the interactive shell, has no __file__.

nodes.label: Interpreter location
nodes.body: sys.executable contains the full path and file name of the Python interpreter program itself, and sys.version the string that appears at the top of the interactive shell with the interpreter's version (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: sys.executable contains the full path and file name of the Python interpreter program itself, and sys.version the string that appears at the top of the interactive shell with the interpreter's version (Sweigart, 2025).

Inside an activated venv sys.executable names the environment's python, which is a quick way to see which interpreter a launcher started; the course's programs also pass sys.executable to subprocess to start another run of the very same Python, the in-program form of running pip as a module. For comparing versions, the version info tuple is easier than this string.

nodes.definition: sys.executable holds the full path of the Python interpreter running the program and sys.version the version text that the interactive shell prints at its top.

nodes.label: Platform checks
nodes.body: One script can run on several operating systems if it asks which one it is on and which Python version runs it (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: One script can run on several operating systems if it asks which one it is on and which Python version runs it (Sweigart, 2025).

Version info covers sys.version_info and comparing versions as tuples. Operating system name covers os.name and sys.platform, which choose between Windows commands such as cls and macOS or Linux commands such as clear.

nodes.label: Version info
nodes.body: sys.version_info.major and sys.version_info.minor are integers, 3 and 13 on the author's laptop running Python 3.13.1, and list(sys.version_info) gives more detail; the chapter prints that list as [3, 13, 1 'final', 0], where a comma after the 1 is missing, and the form is easier to work with than the sys.version string (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: sys.version_info.major and sys.version_info.minor are integers, 3 and 13 on the author's laptop running Python 3.13.1, and list(sys.version_info) gives more detail; the chapter prints that list as [3, 13, 1 'final', 0], where a comma after the 1 is missing, and the form is easier to work with than the sys.version string (Sweigart, 2025).

Under Python 3.14.6, list(sys.version_info) gave [3, 14, 6, 'final', 0], and sys.version_info >= (3, 9) was True, because tuples compare item by item; that one comparison guards code that needs the absolute file variable of Python 3.9 or newer. A program that needs a newer Python than the one running it can stop with exit with message instead of failing later with a confusing error.

nodes.definition: sys.version_info holds the interpreter's version as integers, major and minor first, so sys.version_info >= (3, 9) compares versions directly instead of pulling numbers out of the sys.version string.

nodes.label: Operating system name
nodes.body: os.name is 'nt' on Windows and 'posix' on macOS and Linux, enough for a script that runs different code per family of operating systems, and sys.platform is more specific: 'win32' on Windows, 'darwin' on macOS and 'linux' on Linux; the platform module reports the operating system version and processor in detail (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: os.name is 'nt' on Windows and 'posix' on macOS and Linux, enough for a script that runs different code per family of operating systems, and sys.platform is more specific: 'win32' on Windows, 'darwin' on macOS and 'linux' on Linux; the platform module reports the operating system version and processor in detail (Sweigart, 2025).

On the Ubuntu machine that built this course, Python 3.14.6 gave 'posix' and 'linux'. The best-known use of os.name is the one-line terminal clearing function, which runs cls on Windows and clear elsewhere; launcher files are the other place where the operating system decides everything, since a batch file, a command file and a shell script launcher are three different files for one Python script.

nodes.definition: os.name is 'nt' on Windows and 'posix' on macOS and Linux, and sys.platform is finer grained, 'win32', 'darwin' or 'linux', so a program can run different code on each operating system.

nodes.label: Module checks
nodes.body: A program can check that what it needs is there before it starts its work: a missing third-party module is caught with ModuleNotFoundError, and sys.exit() ends the program with a message the user can act on (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A program can check that what it needs is there before it starts its work: a missing third-party module is caught with ModuleNotFoundError, and sys.exit() ends the program with a message the user can act on (Sweigart, 2025).

Missing module covers the try block around an import statement. Exit with message covers sys.exit() and the exit code the terminal sees, the same channel the chapter's Unix philosophy uses to report success or failure without printing anything.

nodes.label: Missing module
nodes.body: To check whether a module is installed, the import statement goes into a try block whose except clause catches ModuleNotFoundError; if the module is necessary, a descriptive message and a call to sys.exit() are more helpful to the user than a generic error and traceback (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: To check whether a module is installed, the import statement goes into a try block whose except clause catches ModuleNotFoundError; if the module is necessary, a descriptive message and a call to sys.exit() are more helpful to the user than a generic error and traceback (Sweigart, 2025).

Run under Python 3.14.6, importing nonexistentModule inside such a try block ran the except clause, printing the chapter's own sentence. The check matters most for third-party packages such as pyperclip or Bext, which an earlier python -m pip install must have put into the active venv: running a script in the wrong environment is the usual reason the import fails, and running pip as a module in the right one is the usual fix.

nodes.definition: Putting an import statement in a try block and catching ModuleNotFoundError lets a program say that a package is missing in its own words, instead of stopping with a traceback.

nodes.label: Exit with message
nodes.body: sys.exit() terminates the program, which the chapter recommends after a failed import of a module the program cannot do without (Sweigart, 2025). It works by raising SystemExit; given a string, Python prints the text to standard error and the process ends with exit code 1, while sys.exit() or sys.exit(0) means success (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: sys.exit() terminates the program, which the chapter recommends after a failed import of a module the program cannot do without (Sweigart, 2025). It works by raising SystemExit; given a string, Python prints the text to standard error and the process ends with exit code 1, while sys.exit() or sys.exit(0) means success (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Under Python 3.14.6, a program that called sys.exit('needs pyperclip') printed the text to standard error, nothing to standard output, and ended with exit code 1. The exit code is what the chapter's sound and text notification passage means by communicating success or error without text, and it is what a shell script launcher or another program can test after the script ends.

nodes.definition: sys.exit() ends a program by raising SystemExit; given a string, Python prints the text to standard error and the program ends with exit code 1, which the terminal or another program can test.

nodes.label: Text design
nodes.body: The book's programs use print() and input() through a command line interface rather than windows and buttons, and the chapter gathers the design choices that make such a text-based program pleasant to use: its name, its arguments, the clipboard, colour, clearing, sound, verbosity and small dialog boxes, with the Snowstorm animation as a short program that puts several of them to work (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The book's programs use print() and input() through a command line interface rather than windows and buttons, and the chapter gathers the design choices that make such a text-based program pleasant to use: its name, its arguments, the clipboard, colour, clearing, sound, verbosity and small dialog boxes, with the Snowstorm animation as a short program that puts several of them to work (Sweigart, 2025).

Command line arguments covers how a program is named and configured when it starts. Terminal output covers what it shows while it runs. Snowstorm program covers the chapter's text animation, driven by one argument. Message boxes covers the small dialogs that can replace print() and input() altogether.

nodes.label: Command line arguments
nodes.body: The text typed after a command is its command line arguments, passed to it much as arguments are passed to a function, so that ls exampleFolder lists a different folder from ls alone (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The text typed after a command is its command line arguments, passed to it much as arguments are passed to a function, so that ls exampleFolder lists a different folder from ls alone (Sweigart, 2025).

Short command names covers what a command should be called. Argv list covers how a Python script receives the words, and quoted arguments covers words that contain spaces. Argparse module covers the standard library module the chapter recommends once the combinations of arguments become too many to handle by hand.

nodes.label: Short command names
nodes.body: Source code is read more often than it is written, so variables get long names, but commands are typed more often than they are read, so a command typed a dozen times a day deserves a short name, like cp rather than copy; which, where and an internet search check that the name is not already taken (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Source code is read more often than it is written, so variables get long names, but commands are typed more often than they are read, so a command typed a dozen times a day deserves a short name, like cp rather than copy; which, where and an internet search check that the name is not already taken (Sweigart, 2025).

The chapter's own example is ccwd, short for copy current working directory: the author checked with which ccwd and where ccwd before choosing it. A short name reaches the user through a launcher of the same name in a PATH folder, a batch file on Windows or a shell script launcher on Ubuntu, so the name of the launcher is the name of the command.

nodes.definition: Commands are typed far more often than they are read, so a command a user types many times a day deserves a short name, checked first with which or where and an internet search so that it does not clash with an existing program.

nodes.label: Argv list
nodes.body: Python scripts receive their command line arguments in the sys.argv list: python3 yourScript.py hello world sets it to ['yourScript.py', 'hello', 'world'], the first item is the script's file name, and the rest are the typed words, split at spaces (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Python scripts receive their command line arguments in the sys.argv list: python3 yourScript.py hello world sets it to ['yourScript.py', 'hello', 'world'], the first item is the script's file name, and the rest are the typed words, split at spaces (Sweigart, 2025).

Run under Python 3.14.6, a script started with those words printed exactly that list. The documentation adds that whether the first item is a full path depends on the operating system (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and a launcher shows it: started through the chapter's shell script launcher, the script saw its absolute path first. The snowstorm program's density argument and the ccwd script's folder argument are both read straight from this list, which is the simple case the chapter recommends; argparse takes over when it is not.

nodes.definition: sys.argv is the list of command line arguments a script receives: the script's file name first, then the words typed after it, split at spaces, so python3 yourScript.py hello world gives ['yourScript.py', 'hello', 'world'].

nodes.label: Quoted arguments
nodes.body: Arguments are split at spaces, so a space inside one argument needs quotation marks around it when the command is run: python3 yourScript.py 'hello world' sets sys.argv to ['yourScript.py', 'hello world'] (Sweigart, 2025). Python's shlex.split() splits a command line by the same rules as a POSIX shell (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Arguments are split at spaces, so a space inside one argument needs quotation marks around it when the command is run: python3 yourScript.py 'hello world' sets sys.argv to ['yourScript.py', 'hello world'] (Sweigart, 2025). Python's shlex.split() splits a command line by the same rules as a POSIX shell (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Run under Python 3.14.6, the quoted form reached the script as one item, both when the shell split it and when shlex.split() did. Quoting is also what a launcher must preserve: the argument forwarding of a batch file's %* and of '$@' in a shell script keeps each quoted argument whole, which is why both are written that way rather than as a plain list of words.

nodes.definition: Quotation marks keep a space inside one argument, so the two words arrive as the single item 'hello world'; shlex.split() splits a command line the way a POSIX shell does.

nodes.label: Argparse module
nodes.body: Once a program accepts several arguments, reading sys.argv by hand becomes a pile of edge cases - whether spam eggs means the same as eggs spam, what happens when two exclusive options are both given - and the chapter recommends Python's built-in argparse module instead, leaving it to the documentation (Sweigart, 2025). argparse declares each argument once and parses the list, converts types, fills defaults and writes usage and error messages; in Python 3.14 it also colours its help text and can suggest a mistyped choice (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Once a program accepts several arguments, reading sys.argv by hand becomes a pile of edge cases - whether spam eggs means the same as eggs spam, what happens when two exclusive options are both given - and the chapter recommends Python's built-in argparse module instead, leaving it to the documentation (Sweigart, 2025). argparse declares each argument once and parses the list, converts types, fills defaults and writes usage and error messages; in Python 3.14 it also colours its help text and can suggest a mistyped choice (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Run under Python 3.14.6, a parser declaring an optional integer density with default 4 and a --verbose switch turned ['20', '-v'] into density 20 with verbose on and an empty list into the defaults, and a non-number ended the program with exit code 2 and a usage message, the convention for command line errors. That covers the density argument of the snowstorm program and the switches of sound and text notification at once.

nodes.definition: The argparse module, which the chapter recommends once arguments multiply and leaves to its documentation, declares each argument once and then parses sys.argv, converts types, fills in defaults and writes usage and error messages.

nodes.label: Terminal output
nodes.body: Even limited to text, a program can offer an interface close to a graphical one, and the chapter collects the ways: a text-based user interface, the clipboard as input and output, colour, clearing the screen, and sound and quiet or verbose output (Sweigart, 2025).

Text user interface covers the style itself. Clipboard program design covers programs that never ask for input. Colorful text and terminal clearing cover Bext and the os.system() one-liner. Sound and text notification covers how much a command should say, and when it should say nothing at all.

nodes.label: Text user interface
nodes.body: Before graphical operating systems were common, every program talked to its user in text, and applications such as Norton Commander, shown in the chapter's Figure 12-1, drew panels and menus out of text characters; such programs are called TUI, text-based user interface, applications, and their advantage is simplicity (Sweigart, 2025).

The chapter's own pieces of a TUI are colorful text and screen control from Bext, terminal clearing with cls or clear, and the snowstorm program's animation, which redraws the whole window many times a second. A text user interface still runs in a terminal, so it is started like any terminal command, through a launcher, and it stays open until the user ends it.

nodes.definition: A text-based user interface, or TUI, builds panels, menus and colour out of text characters inside a terminal window, as Norton Commander did for browsing files, and is simpler to program than a graphical user interface.

nodes.label: Clipboard program design
nodes.body: Instead of input(), a program can take its text from the clipboard: it imports pyperclip, calls pyperclip.paste() for the input, works on the text and passes the result to pyperclip.copy(), so a user highlights text, copies it, runs the command and pastes the result; pyperclip is installed with pip and needs xclip on Linux (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Instead of input(), a program can take its text from the clipboard: it imports pyperclip, calls pyperclip.paste() for the input, works on the text and passes the result to pyperclip.copy(), so a user highlights text, copies it, runs the command and pastes the result; pyperclip is installed with pip and needs xclip on Linux (Sweigart, 2025).

Run under Python 3.14.6, the chapter 8 bullet transformation turned two copied lines into two bullet lines, the work step of such a program. This machine has no clipboard - pyperclip 1.11.0 raised PyperclipException - so the course runs the ccwd script and the clipboard polling program against a stand-in module with the same copy() and paste(), and says so wherever it does.

nodes.label: Sound and text notification

nodes.label: Snowstorm program
nodes.body: snowstorm.py animates a snowstorm in the terminal with half-block characters for snow and full blocks for the ground, taking its density from an optional command line argument; the chapter chose it because it is fun rather than practical (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Block characters
nodes.body: The program's snow and ground are block text characters that fill the top half, the bottom half or the whole of one character cell, returned by chr(9600), chr(9604) and chr(9608) and kept in the constants TOP, BOTTOM and FULL because names read better than numbers (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Flipbook animation
nodes.body: Inside an endless while loop the program clears the terminal, loops over 20 rows and 40 columns printing either a random TOP or BOTTOM character or a space with print(..., end=''), ends each row with print(), prints two rows of FULL characters as the ground and a reminder that CTRL-C stops it, and pauses with time.sleep(0.2) before the next frame (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Message boxes
nodes.body: A full graphical interface needs a library such as Tkinter, wxPython or PyQt, but small dialog boxes come from the third-party PyMsgBox package, which uses Tkinter and names its functions after JavaScript's message boxes (Sweigart, 2025).

Alert and confirm covers the boxes that show a message and wait for OK or Cancel. Prompt and password covers the boxes that ask for text. Together they can replace print() and input() for a program that needs only an occasional message or answer.

nodes.label: Deployment
nodes.body: Deployment makes a finished program run in as few keystrokes as possible, without opening Mu; the chapter's recipe is a Scripts folder on PATH, a virtual environment in it, and for each script a small launcher file for the operating system, shown on two short programs, ccwd and the Clipboard Recorder, with PyInstaller as the alternative for computers without Python (Sweigart, 2025).

Launcher files covers the batch file, the command file, the shell script launcher and the desktop entry. Launcher mechanics covers the shebang line, the execute permission, argument forwarding and the pause before the window closes. Ccwd command and Clipboard recorder cover the two programs the chapter writes and deploys on all three systems. Compiling with PyInstaller covers the one-file build, its folders and why the result is large.

nodes.label: Launcher files
nodes.body: For each script the chapter writes one small text file per operating system that activates the Scripts folder's virtual environment, runs the script with the environment's Python and deactivates, so that typing one name runs the program (Sweigart, 2025).

Batch file covers Windows and its Run dialog. Command file covers macOS and Spotlight. Shell script launcher covers Ubuntu and the terminal. Desktop entry covers Ubuntu's Dash, which needs a second small file pointing at the shell script.

nodes.label: Batch file
nodes.body: On Windows, yourScript.bat in the Scripts folder holds four lines: @call %HOMEDRIVE%%HOMEPATH%\Scripts\.venv\Scripts\activate.bat, @python %HOMEDRIVE%%HOMEPATH%\Scripts\yourScript.py %*, @pause and @deactivate; the @ hides each command, call is needed or the rest of the file would not run after activate.bat, and the Run dialog, opened with the Windows key and R, then runs it by name (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: On Windows, yourScript.bat in the Scripts folder holds four lines: @call %HOMEDRIVE%%HOMEPATH%\Scripts\.venv\Scripts\activate.bat, @python %HOMEDRIVE%%HOMEPATH%\Scripts\yourScript.py %*, @pause and @deactivate; the @ hides each command, call is needed or the rest of the file would not run after activate.bat, and the Run dialog, opened with the Windows key and R, then runs it by name (Sweigart, 2025).

%HOMEDRIVE% and %HOMEPATH% make the same file work for any user name, since ~ does not mean the home folder on Windows, and %* is the argument forwarding that the macOS and Linux launchers lack. This course could not run a batch file, having no Windows machine, so these lines are reported as the chapter prints them; the shell script launcher, which it could run, follows the same pattern.

nodes.definition: On Windows a yourScript.bat file in a PATH folder activates the virtual environment with @call, runs the script with %* to forward arguments, keeps the window open with @pause and deactivates; the Run dialog, opened with the Windows key and R, then starts it by name.

nodes.label: Command file
nodes.body: On macOS, a plain-text yourScript.command file in the Scripts folder sources ~/Scripts/.venv/bin/activate, runs python3 ~/Scripts/yourScript.py and deactivates; chmod u+x gives it the execute permission, and Spotlight then runs it by name, which it would not do for yourScript.py, opening that in an editor instead (Sweigart, 2025).

The chapter warns that TextEdit must save it as plain text and may capitalise python3 into Python3, which breaks it, and that Spotlight cannot pass command line arguments, so any must be written into the file. Like the shell script launcher, it has nothing after the script's path, so typed arguments are not forwarded either; this course had no macOS machine and did not run one.

nodes.label: Shell script launcher
nodes.body: On Ubuntu, a text file named yourScript with no extension holds #!/usr/bin/env bash, source ~/Scripts/.venv/bin/activate, python3 ~/Scripts/yourScript.py, read -p 'Press any key to continue...' -n1 -s and deactivate; chmod u+x makes it executable, after which typing yourScript in any terminal runs it (Sweigart, 2025).

The online chapter prints the read line's last option with an en dash, which the pause before close concept takes up.

nodes.label: Desktop entry
nodes.body: To run the shell script from Ubuntu's Dash, a yourScript.desktop file in ~/.local/share/applications holds [Desktop Entry], Name=yourScript, Exec=gnome-terminal -- /home/al/Scripts/yourScript and Type=Application; the Exec line must spell out /home/al because ~ is not expanded in this file, and CTRL-H shows the hidden .local folder in a save dialog (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Launcher mechanics
nodes.body: Four details make a launcher work or fail: the first line that names its interpreter, the permission to execute it, passing on the arguments typed after its name, and keeping its window open long enough to read the output (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Four details make a launcher work or fail: the first line that names its interpreter, the permission to execute it, passing on the arguments typed after its name, and keeping its window open long enough to read the output (Sweigart, 2025).

Shebang line and execute permission cover how macOS and Linux run a text file as a program. Argument forwarding covers %* and its missing counterpart. Pause before close covers @pause and read -p, and a typesetting slip in the online chapter that breaks the latter.

nodes.label: Shebang line
nodes.body: The first line of the Ubuntu launcher, #!/usr/bin/env bash, identifies the file as a shell script, so it needs no .sh extension (Sweigart, 2025); a first line beginning with #! names the interpreter that the operating system runs the file with, and the form /usr/bin/env bash asks the env program to find bash on PATH rather than naming its folder.

paras.text: The first line of the Ubuntu launcher, #!/usr/bin/env bash, identifies the file as a shell script, so it needs no .sh extension (Sweigart, 2025); a first line beginning with #! names the interpreter that the operating system runs the file with, and the form /usr/bin/env bash asks the env program to find bash on PATH rather than naming its folder.

Split after its two first characters, the line gives the program /usr/bin/env and its argument bash, the pair the system starts. Dennis Ritchie added this kernel feature at Bell Labs in January 1980, as the story of this chapter tells. A shebang line alone is not enough: the execute permission must also be set, which is why every shell script launcher is followed by chmod u+x.

nodes.definition: A first line that starts with #! names the interpreter the operating system runs the file with; #!/usr/bin/env bash asks the env program to find bash on PATH, so the file needs no .sh extension.

nodes.label: Execute permission
nodes.body: chmod u+x adds execute permission for the file's owner, so that macOS can run a .command file from Spotlight and Linux can run a shell script by name; without it the system refuses to run the file (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: chmod u+x adds execute permission for the file's owner, so that macOS can run a .command file from Spotlight and Linux can run a shell script by name; without it the system refuses to run the file (Sweigart, 2025).

Under Python 3.14.6, stat.filemode() showed the mode -rw-r--r-- of a new file becoming -rwxr--r-- with the owner's execute bit added, the same string the shell script launcher of this course showed after chmod u+x on the Ubuntu machine that built it. The permission and the shebang line together are what let the path search order find and run a launcher kept in the Scripts folder.

nodes.definition: chmod u+x adds the execute permission for the file's owner, without which macOS and Linux refuse to run a launcher; it sets the owner's x bit, turning -rw-r--r-- into -rwxr--r--.

nodes.label: Argument forwarding
nodes.body: The batch file runs @python ...\yourScript.py %*, and %* forwards every command line argument the batch file received to the Python program; the chapter advises always including it in case arguments are added later (Sweigart, 2025). Its macOS command file and Ubuntu shell script launcher, however, run python3 ~/Scripts/yourScript.py with nothing after it.

Run on Ubuntu, that launcher, started as yourScript spam eggs, gave the script no arguments at all, and adding '$@' to its python3 line forwarded both; the same is true of the chapter's ccwd launcher, so ccwd .. as deployed on macOS or Linux copies the current folder, not its parent. Quoted arguments survive '$@' whole, as they survive %*.

nodes.label: Pause before close
nodes.body: @pause in the batch file makes Windows display Press any key to continue and wait, and read -p 'Press any key to continue...' -n1 -s does the same in the Ubuntu shell script, so the window opened by the Run dialog or by Dash does not close before its printed output can be read; a program with no printed output, such as ccwd, leaves the line out (Sweigart, 2025).

The same slip turns python -m into a file name, as running pip as a module explains.

nodes.definition: A pause at the end of a launcher, @pause on Windows or read -p on Ubuntu, keeps the window open after the program ends so that its output can be read; a launcher for a program that prints nothing leaves it out.

nodes.label: Ccwd command
nodes.body: ccwd, short for copy current working directory, copies the folder a terminal is in to the clipboard, for example to paste into a Save File dialog, and takes an optional relative path such as .. to copy another folder instead (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: ccwd, short for copy current working directory, copies the folder a terminal is in to the clipboard, for example to paste into a Save File dialog, and takes an optional relative path such as .. to copy another folder instead (Sweigart, 2025).

Ccwd script covers the four lines and how they use sys.argv and the clipboard. Program working directory covers why the program's os.chdir() does not move the terminal that started it. Its launchers are the chapter's batch file, command file and shell script launcher, written for ccwd.py.

nodes.label: Ccwd script
nodes.body: ccwd.py reads: import pyperclip, os, sys; if len(sys.argv) > 1: os.chdir(sys.argv[1]); pyperclip.copy(os.getcwd()); sys.argv always holds at least the script's name, so more than one item means the user gave a folder, and the batch file for it has no @pause because it prints nothing (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Program working directory
nodes.body: Every program has its own current working directory setting, and changing it with os.chdir() does not change the current working directory of the terminal that ran the program (Sweigart, 2025); a new process starts in its parent's folder, and what it does with its own folder afterwards stays inside it (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Run for this course, a shell in ~/Scripts started a Python program that moved to .. and printed ~, and the shell's own pwd afterwards still printed ~/Scripts. That is why the ccwd script can move freely before it copies, and why change directory in a launcher or a script never surprises the user's terminal.

nodes.definition: Every running program has its own current working directory, so os.chdir() inside ccwd.py does not move the terminal that started it; after ccwd .. the terminal is still in the folder it was in.

nodes.label: Clipboard recorder
nodes.body: The Clipboard Recorder, cliprec.py, turns copying many links from a web page into a two-step job: it watches the clipboard and prints every new text copied, so the user only copies links and finally copies everything from its window at once (Sweigart, 2025).

Clipboard polling covers the loop that notices new text. Keyboard interrupt exit covers how the program ends when the user presses CTRL-C. Its Ubuntu desktop entry is named Clipboard Recorder, which is the name Dash shows.

nodes.label: Clipboard polling
nodes.body: cliprec.py prints Recording clipboard... (Ctrl-C to stop), keeps previous_content = '', and in an endless loop calls pyperclip.paste(), prints the content and stores it when it differs from previous_content, then sleeps 0.01 seconds, so the loop checks the clipboard a hundred times a second instead of tens of thousands of times and does not hog the CPU (Sweigart, 2025).

The loop ends only through a keyboard interrupt exit.

nodes.definition: cliprec.py reads the clipboard in an endless loop, prints the text only when it differs from previous_content, and sleeps 0.01 seconds between reads so that it checks a hundred times a second instead of hogging the CPU.

nodes.body: The loop of cliprec.py sits inside a try block; pressing CTRL-C raises KeyboardInterrupt, the except KeyboardInterrupt clause holds only pass, a statement that does nothing but fills a block that needs one, and the program ends without a traceback (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.body: PyInstaller is installed with pip install pyinstaller, and python -m PyInstaller --onefile yourScript.py, with python3 on macOS and Linux, compiles the script; PyInstaller must be typed with a capital P and a capital I or the command fails with No module named pyinstaller, and --onefile has two dashes (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Build and dist
nodes.body: After PyInstaller runs there is a build folder, which can be deleted, and a dist folder containing the executable, which needs no virtual environment and can be copied to other computers; PyInstaller must run on the operating system the executable is for, so a Windows build makes only a Windows program (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.definition: PyInstaller leaves a build folder, which can be deleted, and a dist folder holding the executable, which runs without Python or a virtual environment on a computer with the same operating system as the one that built it.

lecture.title: Chapter 12: Command Line Programs
lecture.say: Every program so far has been started from the code editor. This chapter takes programs out of the editor and into the terminal: how the terminal finds a program, how a virtual environment keeps each program's packages apart, how a program reads the words typed after its name, how its text interface should behave, and how a small launcher file or PyInstaller turns a script into a command anyone can run. Every example on these slides was run under Python 3.14.6 on Ubuntu, and the result printed beside it is the result Python gave on that machine.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has six parts. It starts with the terminal and the PATH variable that lets it find a program, moves to virtual environments and pip, then to programs that know about themselves and read their command line arguments, then to the design of a text interface, with the snowstorm animation, and then to deployment with launcher files, the chapter's two short programs and PyInstaller, and ends with the summary and resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need, and four of the slides are true stories that explain where a piece of this chapter's vocabulary came from.

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The first question is the chapter's spine: a typed name is looked up in the folders of PATH, it usually finds a small launcher file, the launcher activates a virtual environment and starts the interpreter, and the interpreter hands the typed words to the program in sys.argv. Each step can fail in its own way, and this deck runs every step to show where. The second question is the deck's watch-out: the chapter was written for Python 3.13 and three operating systems, and a few of its printed lines differ on Python 3.14 or Ubuntu today, from the packages a new environment holds to an en dash where a hyphen belongs. The chips give the size of the chapter.

lecture.title: The terminal: cd, pwd, dir and ls
lecture.say: The terminal has a current working directory, shown in its prompt: cd followed by a path changes it, pwd on macOS and Linux or cd alone on Windows shows it, and dir on Windows or ls on macOS and Linux lists what it holds. A Python program does the same with os.chdir(), os.getcwd() and os.listdir(), as this console shows, and dir *.exe becomes a test on the .exe ending. A program in the current folder runs as example.exe on Windows but must be typed as ./example on macOS and Linux. The chips are six of the chapter's seven words for a program, the seventh being app: a script is run by an interpreter from its source, a command is run from a terminal with its options given up front, and a shell script is a file of terminal commands, the form of every launcher later in this deck.

lecture.title: PATH: how the terminal finds a program
lecture.say: PATH is an environment variable holding a list of folders, separated by colons on macOS and Linux and by semicolons on Windows. When a name is typed, the terminal looks in each folder in order and runs the first match, which is why which python3 or where python is the way to find out which program a name really starts. The console builds a small PATH of two folders, a and b, and shutil.which, Python's own which, finds spam in b although a holds a spam of its own one level down, because folders inside a PATH folder are never searched. Adding a folder to PATH is the chapter's first step towards deployment: once the Scripts folder is on PATH, any launcher placed there runs by its bare name from any folder.

lecture.title: Virtual environments: python -m venv .venv
lecture.say: python -m venv .venv makes a separate Python installation in a hidden folder named .venv, with its own set of installed packages, so two programs that need different versions of one package can each have their own. This program really creates one. The folder holds bin with the activate script, pyvenv.cfg, which keeps the original installation's packages out, and, new since Python 3.13, a .gitignore. Inside it pip list shows pip alone: the chapter's own listing also shows setuptools, which Python stopped installing into new environments in version 3.12. Activation, with source activate on macOS and Linux or activate.bat on Windows, puts the environment's folder first on PATH in that one terminal window; the last two lines are the test a running program can make itself, sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix, False outside and True inside.

lecture.title: pip began as pyinstall in September 2008
lecture.say: Ian Bicking, who had already written virtualenv, announced a new installer called pyinstall in a post titled 'pyinstall: A New Hope' on 24 September 2008, as an alternative to easy_install. On 28 October 2008 he renamed it in a post titled 'pyinstall is dead, long live pip!', and pip, by Bicking's own account a recursive acronym for Pip Installs Packages, became the installer Python now ships with. Carl Meyer then wrote PEP 405, created on 13 June 2011, which named Bicking's virtualenv as the tool that had shown the value of isolated environments and made them part of Python 3.3 as the venv module. The chapter's two commands, python -m venv .venv and python -m pip install, are those two pieces of work side by side. The account rests on these sources.
